newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus presses on with crackdown on journalists.
newsitem.headline: Belarus presses on with crackdown on journalists.

text.p: A mounting row over press freedom between Russia and Belarus has thrown a cloud over efforts by the two former Soviet republics to seek closer integration leading to an eventual union.
On Thursday Belarus police briefly detained 14 journalists working for local and foreign media who were covering the handing in of a petition in support of an arrested Russian television crew.
The journalists were later released and were scheduled to appear in court on Friday on charges of violating tough restrictions on public rallies introduced by President Alexander Lukashenko.

The petition called for the release of a crew from Russia's mainly state-owned ORT network, detained by border guards on Saturday accused of illegally crossing the Belarus-Lithuanian border, and held in the border town of Grodno.
ORT correspondent Pavel Sheremet had already been accused by the Belarussian authorities earlier this month of biased reporting and stripped of his official press accreditation.
The incident sparked a harsh exchange between Lukashenko and Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who signed a series of accords in May on closer integration leading to possible union.

Yeltsin said on Wednesday he was "surprised and indignant" at the arrests and suggested Moscow might revise the union charter, which was watered down by Moscow liberals who feared it could give Lukashenko too much say in Kremlin policy.

Lukashenko retorted on Thursday in a television interview, accusing some Russian leaders including First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais of trying to torpedo integration between the two republics.
"I will give my explanations but only after the president of Russia gives his -- on the information warfare which the Russian media is waging against me," Lukashenko said.
He accused Sheremet of being in the pay of foreign intelligence services, but did not name them.
Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, sought to calm the waters by saying Yeltsin did not want the incident to mar overall ties betweeen the two republics.
But he added that Yeltsin wanted press freedoms to be maintained in both states in accordance with the union charter they had signed.
Lukashenko rewrote the constitution in November last year after a landslide win in a referendum which critics said was illegitimate. The new basic law gives him vast powers.
He has closed some newspapers and ousted the editors of others. Some opposition newspapers are now published in Lithuania.
Amnesty International called the ORT journalists "prisoners of conscience" who were being held for carrying out their jobs.
Human Rights Watch, a New York-based human rights group, released a report on Thursday called "Belarus: Crushing Civil Society."

In a summary made available in London, it said the Minsk government's campaign against Russian broadcast media was especially fierce because they dared to criticise its policies and offered the only alternative to state-controlled television.
